### Part 1 · Before you arrive

Accounts and data only. Nothing here needs software installed at home.

1. Confirm you can sign in to Power BI in a browser at [app.powerbi.com](https://app.powerbi.com) with your NDSU account.
2. Confirm your Smartsheet access works.

::: {.part}
### Part 2 · What you will have at the end

SA8 — histograms before and after, the heuristic code, the LP formulation and solution, the <code>.pod</code>, the ranked comparison
:::

::: {.part}
### Part 3 · Build it yourself — 25 minutes

1. In Colab, build the resource histogram from the Week 6 network plus assignments.
2. Implement the minimum-slack leveling heuristic yourself. Re-plot the histogram. Record the new finish date.
3. Formulate the same problem as an integer program in PuLP: minimise makespan subject to precedence and resource capacity. Solve it.
4. Record the gap between your heuristic makespan and the optimal one.
:::

::: {.part}
### Part 4 · Now the professional tool — 20 minutes

1. Run ProjectLibre's <em>Level Resources</em> on the same file. Record its finish date and exactly which activities it moved.
2. Generate the time-phased cost baseline and export the S-curve.
3. In Smartsheet, import the schedule, assign resources, and open the resource view. Note what the cloud tool shows a sponsor that the desktop tool does not.
4. <strong>First Power BI session.</strong> Export the assignment table from Smartsheet, load it into Power BI, and build a resource-utilisation matrix — person by week, conditionally formatted so anything over 100% turns red. This is the visual nobody looked at in the case.
:::

::: {.part}
### Part 5 · Where do they disagree? — 15 minutes

Four finish dates now — your heuristic, the solver's, ProjectLibre's, and Smartsheet's. Rank them, explain the gaps, and say which you would commit to a customer. The optimal one may well be the wrong answer.

Write one paragraph. **This is the graded part** — it is the only thing here a machine cannot check.
:::

::: {.part}
### Part 6 · Run the check

Run the `verify()` cell at the end of the notebook. It tests your own outputs against tolerances and
prints a completion code. If it fails, you have found your error while it is still cheap to fix —
that is the point of it. Paste the code into your submission.
:::

::: {.part}
### Part 7 · Done looks like — the checklist your neighbour runs on you at minute 65

- [ ] Four finish dates recorded
- [ ] the LP is provably optimal or the solver's gap is reported
- [ ] the S-curve is a curve, not a straight line
:::
